transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, yeah, so I came in because I just feel like I absolutely cannot get my schoolwork and my little accessories shop organized at the same time. It's just a mess. My supplies, my due dates for classes, receipts, assignment notes... they all just end up in these massive piles everywhere, and I stare at them and I don't even know what to do first. Actually, speaking of my shop, I just got this huge shipment of these really cute resin charms in yesterday—like little strawberries and clouds, they're so adorable. I was supposed to sort them by color, but then my cat, Barnaby, he knocked the entire box off the table, and they went everywhere. It took me like two hours to find them all under the couch, and I found a bunch of old hair ties down there too, which is weird because I haven't bought that brand of hair ties since, like, sophomore year of high school. But yeah, the piles. It's just really overwhelming.

When you look at those piles of schoolwork and shop supplies, what bothers you more—that you can't seem to focus long enough to sort through them, or that you're worried about missing deadlines and falling behind?

Um, I'm not really sure which one is worse, honestly. Like, I look at them and I know I have a deadline coming up, so I sit down to do it, but then... I don't know, it's just all bad. Like last week I had this short essay due, and I went to submit it on the school portal, but the website was acting up. It was so annoying. Have you ever tried to use those online student portals? They are literally always crashing. 

Anyway, while I was waiting for the page to load, I started looking at these custom packaging boxes for my shop because I really want to upgrade from just the plain pink bubble mailers. I found these holographic ones that are so pretty, but shipping from overseas is crazy expensive right now. I ended up reading this whole long article about the global shipping supply chain and how cargo containers actually get lost at sea all the time. There are like thousands of them just sitting at the bottom of the ocean right now. Imagine what's in them! Like, there could be a whole container of vintage clothes or electronics just hanging out with the fish. 

Wait... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the piles. Yeah, so, I don't really know which part of it bothers me more. I just know I can't seem to get through them.

When you actually sit down and try to work on one of those piles—say, sorting the charms or writing an assignment—can you concentrate on that one task for a reasonable amount of time, or do you find your mind jumping to other things even when you're trying to focus?

Um, yeah, I mean... I try to concentrate, I really do. Like, if I'm in class or even just watching one of those video lectures for my business assignments, I'll start out totally focused. I'm listening, I'm taking notes with my favorite pen—it's this really nice gel pen I got from a stationery store in Little Tokyo, it has a tiny little cat on the cap and it writes so smooth. I actually bought like five of them because I'm always losing pens. Do you ever do that? Just buy a bunch of something because you know you'll lose it? 

But anyway, yeah, I'll be listening, and then maybe like... five minutes in, my brain is just somewhere else entirely. I'll start thinking about a new design for a keychain, or like, how I should package my next batch of orders, and then suddenly the video is over or the professor is moving on to the next slide, and I realize I completely missed half of what they just said. It's so frustrating because I really wanted to hear it, but my brain just... took a detour, I guess. Like yesterday, I was watching a video on inventory management, and the guy in the video was wearing this really weird tie. It had tiny little ducks on it. And I started wondering where you even buy a tie with ducks on it, and if his kids bought it for him for Father's Day, and before I knew it, I was Googling duck ties instead of learning about spreadsheets. So... yeah, my mind definitely jumps around a lot.

How far back do you remember having these kinds of attention problems? Like, do you remember struggling to focus and getting distracted like this back in elementary school or middle school, or is this something that's more of a recent thing?

Um, yeah, no, it's definitely not a recent thing at all. It goes way, way back. Like, my mom actually still has all these old notes from my teachers from back in elementary school. She keeps literally everything in these huge plastic bins in the garage, which honestly stresses me out because spiders get into them. I hate spiders so much. Once I found a huge wolf spider in my bedroom and I literally slept on the living room couch for three days. 

But yeah, her bins. She has these old notes that say I was basically always out of my seat, and I was always talking before the teacher even called on me. And apparently I would just rush through all the group activities, even when I totally understood the work, just to get it done. I remember one of those group projects was about the solar system, and we had to paint these little styrofoam balls, and I got blue paint all over my favorite overalls. They were those really cool corduroy ones? I was so mad because I wanted to wear them for school picture day, and my mom tried to bleach the stain out but it just turned this weird bright pink color. 

But wait, what was I... oh, yeah. The attention stuff. So, yeah, it's been happening since I was little, for sure.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong history of inattention, distractibility, and impulsivity beginning in elementary school. She demonstrates persistent difficulty sustaining attention during tasks (lectures, videos, assignments), with mind frequently wandering to unrelated topics. She exhibits poor organization, excessive tangentiality in speech, difficulty completing tasks, and significant functional impairment in both academic and occupational (shop) domains. The early onset (elementary school), chronic course, and pervasive nature across multiple settings support ADHD, Combined or Predominantly Inattentive Type. F90.9 (ADHD, unspecified) is assigned due to insufficient information to definitively distinguish between subtypes, though predominantly inattentive features are prominent.
